disease_info: Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) is characterized by persistent, excessive worry and apprehensive expectation about multiple life domains (such as work, health, finances, or family) occurring more days than not for at least several months. The worry is typically experienced as difficult to control and is accompanied by physical and cognitive manifestations like fatigue, muscle tension, restlessness, difficulty concentrating, and sleep disturbance. It often has a chronic, fluctuating course, with periods of exacerbation in response to stressors but without being limited to discrete panic attacks or specific feared situations. Clinically, GAD is distinguished from normal worry by its pervasiveness, duration, and degree of impairment, and from other anxiety disorders by the broad range of concerns rather than a focus on particular phobic objects, panic episodes, or traumatic triggers.

narrative.stressor: About eight months ago, Ronny’s school district underwent a major curriculum overhaul and introduced a new data-driven evaluation system that tied teacher performance reviews to standardized test gains and extensive documentation. As the unofficial organizer for the robotics club, community theater, and several mentoring commitments, he found himself staying later and later to redesign lessons, track metrics, and respond to a flood of emails, while still trying to keep up with baseball league games and rehearsals he had promised to direct. Over roughly seven months, the constant sense that he might miss a deadline, overlook a safety protocol, or let down students and colleagues began to spill into his evenings and weekends, crowding out the enjoyment he usually derived from his meticulously planned hobbies and straining his patience at home when his wife and son asked for his attention. He finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after his principal gently pointed out that he seemed increasingly preoccupied and scattered in meetings, and his wife expressed concern that his mounting unease about work was starting to overshadow family time and even derail a long-planned summer road trip.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind just never shuts off—I feel like I can’t stop worrying about school and everything I’m responsible for, no matter what I do.”

narrative.stressor: Roughly nine months ago, Sonia’s husband was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and mild congestive heart failure, and she took on the role of coordinating his medications, dietary changes, and frequent medical appointments. At the same time, she was heavily involved in planning the new multicultural senior art center, running her book club, and helping with community garden responsibilities, leaving her feeling increasingly stretched between caregiving duties and longstanding community commitments. Over the next seven months, she found herself double- and triple-checking pill organizers, second-guessing every meal she cooked for her husband, and rearranging museum tours and garden work when appointments shifted, which gradually eroded the sense of enjoyment she usually derived from her cultural activities. She ultimately sought psychiatric care after her primary care physician noticed how tense and keyed up she appeared during a routine visit, and she admitted that the strain of managing her husband’s health and her many roles had become overwhelming and was starting to sap the pleasure from her retirement.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m constantly bracing myself—my whole body stays tight all day from worrying about my husband and everything I’m juggling.”

narrative.stressor: Seven to eight months ago, Alejandro transitioned from a more structured academic program into a demanding full-time analytical chemistry position at a lab focused on sustainable polymers, where project timelines were tight and expectations for independent work were high. Wanting to prove himself as a first-generation Salvadoran-American in a competitive STEM environment, he volunteered for extra data analysis, drafted bilingual reports for international collaborators, and continued his community outreach teaching chemistry to middle-school students on weekends. As grant deadlines and instrument maintenance issues piled up, he began spending long hours rechecking his SEM and XRD outputs and replaying minor lab mishaps in his mind, which started to intrude on his painting sessions, hikes, and even his calls home to family in El Salvador. When his supervisor gently raised concerns about his declining productivity despite the extra time he was putting in, and he realized he was coming home from the lab too drained to cook or paint and dreading the next workday for months on end, he decided to seek psychiatric evaluation through the employee assistance program.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m exhausted all the time, like I’m worn out before the day even starts, and I can’t seem to get my energy back.”
